blocks.text: An indexed heap, also called an indexed priority queue, is a plain binary heap with one extra piece of bookkeeping attached to it: a map from each element's original identity to the position that element currently occupies inside the heap array. That single addition unlocks an operation a plain heap cannot support efficiently at all, changing the priority of an element that is already sitting somewhere inside the heap.

This operation is usually called decreaseKey (for a min-heap) or increaseKey (for a max-heap), and it shows up constantly in graph algorithms. Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm both repeatedly discover a better estimate for a node that is already waiting inside the priority queue, and both need a fast way to update that node's priority in place rather than removing it and starting over.

A plain heap array only exposes efficient access to the element at the very top. It has no concept of identity: given a node label like D, there is no shortcut to find where D currently lives inside the array, other than scanning every slot. An indexed heap fixes exactly that gap.

items: Plain heap: supports insert and extractMin/extractMax in O(log n), but locating an arbitrary element by its identity costs O(n).
Indexed heap: adds an O(1) identity to position lookup on top of the same heap, so decreaseKey/increaseKey becomes an O(log n) operation instead of an O(n) one.

blocks.text: The rest of this topic builds up the position map, walks through a worked decreaseKey example, and implements the whole structure from scratch in C++.

content.title: 1. The Problem a Plain Heap Cannot Solve Efficiently

blocks.text: Consider Dijkstra's algorithm. Every node starts with a tentative shortest path distance of infinity, except the source, which starts at zero. Nodes are pushed into a min-heap keyed by their tentative distance, and the algorithm repeatedly pops the node with the smallest tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges.

Relaxing an edge sometimes discovers a shorter path to a node that is already sitting inside the heap, one that has not been popped yet. When that happens, the algorithm needs to lower that node's key inside the heap so it gets popped earlier, in the correct priority order.

This is where a plain heap runs into trouble. A binary heap array only guarantees fast access to the element at index 0, the minimum. It does not know, and cannot cheaply answer, the question of at what index the entry for node D currently lives. The heap property only constrains parent and child relationships; it says nothing about where a specific identity ended up after a sequence of inserts, sifts, and extractions.

Without extra bookkeeping, the only way to find node D inside a plain heap array is a linear scan through every slot until a match is found. Once found, updating its key and sifting it up or down still takes O(log n), but the search that precedes it costs O(n). For a graph with V vertices and E edges, doing this scan on every relaxed edge turns an algorithm that should run in roughly O(E log V) into something far slower.

The entire value proposition of an indexed heap is removing that O(n) scan. Everything else, sift up, sift down, extractMin, is identical to a plain heap. The only new capability is answering where element X currently sits, in O(1).

items: Plain heap decreaseKey: O(n) to find the element, plus O(log n) to restore the heap property, so O(n) overall.
Indexed heap decreaseKey: O(1) to find the element via the position map, plus O(log n) to restore the heap property, so O(log n) overall.

content.title: 2. The Core Idea: A Position Map on Top of a Heap

blocks.text: An indexed heap keeps the exact same underlying array and the exact same sift up / sift down logic as a plain binary heap. What it adds is a second array, usually called position[], that maps each element's original identity to the index that element currently occupies inside the heap array.

Concretely, if node D is currently sitting at index 3 of the heap array, then position[D] = 3. Whenever D moves, because it got swapped during a sift up or a sift down, position[D] is updated to reflect its new index. The map is kept perfectly in sync with the array at every single step, not just at the start or the end of an operation.

blocks.caption: The position map points from an identity to its current heap array index; the heap array itself points back from index to identity.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865013-171914632.png
blocks.alt: The Core Idea: A Position Map on Top of a Heap

blocks.text: With this map in place, decreaseKey(D, newValue) becomes a two step operation. First, look up position[D] to get D's current index directly, in O(1). Second, update D's key at that index and sift it up, since the key got smaller, until the heap property is restored, in O(log n). There is no scanning step anymore.
Why not just store data at a fixed index instead?

A natural question is why not skip the heap array reshuffling altogether and keep every element at a fixed, identity based index. The answer is that a heap's efficiency comes precisely from being a compact, complete binary tree stored in array form, where sifting is a simple O(log n) walk up or down the implicit tree. Fixing every element's position would break that tree structure and make the heap property impossible to maintain efficiently. The position map is a compromise: the heap array is still free to reorganize itself however it needs to, and the map simply tracks where everything ended up.

content.title: 3. Two Parallel Mappings and Why Both Directions Matter

blocks.text: A working indexed heap actually needs bookkeeping in both directions, not just one. The two pieces are usually described as:

items: position[]: identity to current heap index. Given an element's original identity, find out where it currently sits in the array. This is what makes decreaseKey fast.
heap[] itself, or a separate heapIndexToIdentity[]: current heap index to identity. Given an array index, find out which element's identity is stored there.

blocks.text: In most implementations the second direction does not need a brand new array at all. If the heap array stores identities directly, so heap[i] is literally the identity of whatever sits at index i, then the heap array already is the index to identity map. Some textbook implementations instead store full key/value structs inside the heap array and keep a separate parallel array purely for the index to identity direction; the idea is identical either way, only the storage layout differs.

Both directions are required because of what happens during a single swap. When a sift up or sift down swaps the elements at heap indices i and j, two things must happen together: the two identities must trade places inside the heap array, which is the index to identity direction, and position[] must be updated for both identities to reflect their new indices, which is the identity to index direction. Skipping either half leaves the structure inconsistent.

Read that swap function carefully. std::swap(heap[i], heap[j]) handles the index to identity direction automatically, since the array slots themselves now hold the other identity. The two lines directly after it handle the identity to index direction explicitly, by writing the new index into position[] for whichever identities just moved. If that swap helper is the only place where indices ever change, and every sift up and sift down routes every exchange through it, the two mappings can never drift out of sync.

content.title: 4. Worked Example: decreaseKey in a Dijkstra Style Run

blocks.text: Suppose Dijkstra's algorithm is mid run and the min-heap currently holds five graph nodes, each keyed by its tentative shortest path distance from the source. The heap array, 0-indexed, and the position map look like this:

Reading the array as a tree: index 0 is the root, A, with distance 2. Index 1 (C, distance 4) and index 2 (B, distance 9) are its children. Index 3 (D, distance 15) and index 4 (E, distance 7) are children of index 1. The heap property holds throughout the array: every parent's distance is less than or equal to both of its children's distances.
At this point position[A]=0, position[C]=1, position[B]=2, position[D]=3, and position[E]=4, matching the array exactly.

Now suppose the algorithm is relaxing the edges out of node C and discovers a path to D through C with total length 3, far shorter than D's current tentative distance of 15. Dijkstra calls decreaseKey(D, 3).

items: Look up position[D]. It returns 3 directly, in O(1). No scanning through the array is needed.
Update D's stored distance from 15 to 3 at heap index 3.

Sift D up: its parent sits at index (3 minus 1) divided by 2, which is index 1, holding C with distance 4. Since D's new distance, 3, is smaller than C's distance, 4, swap indices 1 and 3. Update position[D] to 1 and position[C] to 3.
Continue sifting from D's new index, 1. Its parent sits at index 0, holding A with distance 2. Since D's distance, 3, is not smaller than A's distance, 2, the sift stops here.
D now sits at index 1, and position[D] = 1. Total work for the whole operation: one O(1) lookup plus a single swap, comfortably inside O(log n).

blocks.caption: Tracing decreaseKey(D, 3): the position map finds D in O(1), then a single sift-up swap restores the heap property.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865014-519378811.png
blocks.alt: Worked Example: decreaseKey in a Dijkstra Style Run

blocks.text: On a heap of only five elements the difference between an O(1) lookup and an O(n) scan is not dramatic. Picture the same trace on a road network with a hundred thousand intersections instead: the position map still answers position[D] instantly, while a plain heap would need to scan through, on average, tens of thousands of array slots before it even started sifting.

content.title: 5. C++ Implementation of an Indexed Min Heap

blocks.text: The implementation below stores three parallel arrays sized to the number of possible identities, n. heap[] stores which identity sits at each heap index, doubling as the index to identity direction. position[] stores the current heap index for each identity, with -1 meaning that identity is not currently in the heap. dist[] stores the actual priority value, the key, for each identity.

The swapNodes helper from the previous section is the only place indices ever move, so siftUp, siftDown, and extractMin can all call it without worrying about keeping position[] in sync themselves. decreaseKey is deliberately the shortest method in the class: an O(1) lookup through position[] followed by a single call to siftUp. That brevity is the entire point of the structure.
A typical Dijkstra loop uses contains to decide whether a node is being seen for the first time, which calls insert, or has already been queued with a worse distance, which calls decreaseKey instead:
This loop never pushes a duplicate entry for the same node. At every moment, the heap contains at most one entry per graph node, and that entry always reflects the best distance discovered so far.

Every operation on an indexed heap costs the same as the equivalent plain heap operation, with one crucial exception. Insert still costs O(log n) for the sift up. ExtractMin still costs O(log n) for the sift down. Peeking the minimum is still O(1). The exception is decreaseKey, which drops from O(n) on a plain heap down to O(log n) on an indexed heap, because the O(n) search is replaced by an O(1) map lookup.

blocks.text: The cost of this improvement is a constant factor of extra bookkeeping: one additional integer array of size n, and a few extra array writes inside every swap. In exchange, an algorithm that calls decreaseKey once per edge, such as Dijkstra on a graph with E edges, drops from O(E times n) in the worst case down to O(E log n), which for dense or large graphs is the difference between a solution finishing in milliseconds and one that times out.
The headline number to remember: decreaseKey goes from O(n) to O(log n). Everything else about an indexed heap is exactly as fast, and exactly as slow, as a plain heap.

content.title: 7. Why This Matters for Dijkstra's and Prim's Algorithm

blocks.text: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm share the same underlying shape: repeatedly pull the smallest keyed element out of a priority queue, then possibly lower the key of some other element still waiting inside that same queue. In Dijkstra, the key is a tentative shortest path distance. In Prim, the key is the minimum weight edge connecting a node to the growing spanning tree. Both algorithms depend on decreaseKey to hit their textbook O(E log V) time bound.

Standard library priority queues, C++'s priority_queue, Python's heapq, and Java's PriorityQueue, do not expose a decreaseKey operation at all. The common workaround, called lazy deletion, sidesteps the problem entirely: instead of updating an existing entry, the algorithm simply pushes a brand new entry with the improved key, and leaves the old, now stale entry sitting in the heap.

The if (visited[u]) continue; line is doing all the work that an indexed heap's position[] map would otherwise do more precisely. It lets stale entries sit harmlessly in the heap and simply skips them when they eventually surface at the top, rather than preventing them from existing in the first place.

blocks.text: Both approaches produce the same shortest paths and the same asymptotic O(E log V) bound. Lazy deletion is simpler to write and is what almost every interview solution uses in practice. An indexed heap is more precise, uses less memory in the worst case, and pops fewer stale entries, which matters in systems where the priority queue is doing millions of operations per second, such as network routers or real time pathfinding in a game engine.

items: Forgetting to update position[] on every single swap inside sift up or sift down, not just once at the start or end of the function. Even one missed update silently desynchronizes the map from the array.

Calling insert on an identity that is already inside the heap instead of decreaseKey. This corrupts position[], since the identity now appears to live at two different indices at once. Always check contains(identity) first and branch accordingly.

Calling decreaseKey with a value that is not actually smaller than the current key. Some implementations silently corrupt the heap property if this is not guarded; the safe version simply returns early when the new key is not an improvement.

Forgetting to mark an identity's position as removed, for example setting position[identity] = -1, after extractMin. A later decreaseKey call on an already removed identity should be rejected, not silently operate on stale state.

Confusing which array holds identities and which holds keys. heap[] stores identities, position[] maps identity to index, and a separate dist[] or key array stores the actual priority values. Mixing these three up is a common source of subtle bugs.

blocks.text: The first mistake is the most dangerous because it does not fail loudly. A heap array with a slightly wrong position[] entry still looks like a valid heap from the outside, extractMin still returns elements in the right order, right up until the moment a decreaseKey call uses the stale index and either sifts the wrong element or reads out of bounds. Routing every single index change through one shared swap helper, as shown earlier, is the most reliable way to avoid this class of bug.

Unlike a Fenwick Tree or a segment tree, an indexed heap rarely appears as the direct subject of a standalone interview or contest problem. It is best understood as a building block inside graph algorithms, specifically the structure that gives a textbook correct Dijkstra or Prim implementation its full O(E log V) time bound, since decreaseKey needs to be O(log n) rather than O(n) for that bound to hold.

items: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm: the classic use case, updating a node's tentative distance as shorter paths are discovered.
Prim's Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithm: nearly identical structure, updating a node's minimum connecting edge weight as smaller edges are discovered.

Network Delay Time (LC 743) and Path With Minimum Effort (LC 1631): typical LeetCode Dijkstra variants where the lazy deletion workaround with a plain priority_queue is the expected, accepted solution.
Swim in Rising Water (LC 778): a Prim style / Dijkstra style problem on a grid, again usually solved with lazy deletion rather than a hand rolled indexed heap.

blocks.text: In practice, almost no LeetCode problem requires implementing an indexed heap from scratch. The lazy deletion workaround from the previous section is what interviewers expect by default, since none of the common standard libraries expose decreaseKey. Bringing up the indexed heap unprompted, and being able to explain precisely why it improves the theoretical bound, is a strong signal of deeper graph algorithm understanding, and it matters directly in performance critical systems such as network routers, game engine pathfinding, and simulation schedulers, where the constant factor and memory savings over lazy deletion are not just academic.

blocks.text: An indexed heap is a small structural addition, one extra array and a disciplined swap function, but it is exactly the kind of detail that separates a textbook correct graph algorithm implementation from one that quietly degrades to a slower complexity class under the hood.
